The storm had dragged half the beach into the lighthouse stairwell: kelp, gray sand, a cracked buoy bell that knocked softly whenever the wind shouldered the door. Mara swept until her palms blistered, then climbed to check the lamp. Dawn was still only a pale rumor behind the clouds.

On the gallery outside, wedged beneath the iron rail, she found a bottle stoppered with red wax. That was not so strange; storms delivered bottles, shoes, once even a piano key. But this one held a strip of oilskin folded around a brass button from a coat she had buried with her father twelve years before.

The message was written in his blocky hand: Keep the light for one more night. Mara read it twice, feeling the tower breathe around her. Below, beyond the rocks, something moved in the white water where no boat should have survived. She tucked the note into her sleeve and went inside to trim the wick.
